title: Sharp, positional chest pain in a 34-year-old software engineer
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 34-year-old woman in the ED late at night with sharp pleuritic chest pain that is worse lying down and better sitting forward. The candidate then interprets her observations, ECG, bloods and chest X-ray, gives a differential that covers the life-threatening cardiac, pulmonary and oesophageal causes, and outlines management and safety netting.
focus: Acute chest pain in a young adult: recognising acute pericarditis on history, examination and ECG while excluding its life-threatening mimics
context: Young adult with no cardiovascular risk factors
stem:
You are the intern in the Emergency Department late at night. Farihah Hussain, a 34-year-old software engineer, has come in with chest pain that will not go away. She looks tired and uncomfortable.

Her triage observations are: heart rate 105/min, blood pressure 130/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, temperature 37.8 °C and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Weight 64 kg.

A nurse is with you and can carry out your instructions.
tasks: Take a focused history from Farihah and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you her observations, 12-lead ECG, blood results and chest X-ray report. Interpret them, give your most likely diagnosis and differentials, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Farihah Hussain, a 34-year-old software engineer. It is late at night. You look tired and uncomfortable, and you are sitting on the trolley leaning forward. Answer clearly. You are worried, but you are not panicking. When the candidate says what they would examine, the examiner gives the findings from the Exam findings below.

What the nurse says at the start (if the candidate asks, or straight away if they do not): "Her triage obs are on the chart. She won't lie back on the trolley and keeps sitting forward. I recorded an ECG at 22:48." If the candidate asks for the ECG or blood results during Part 1, the examiner says they will be given in Part 2. If the candidate asks for IV access and bloods, the nurse says, "Cannula's in and bloods are off, including a troponin."

How you change with what the candidate does:

  • If they ask you to lie back flat (for example, to examine you), the pain gets worse, to 8/10: "Ooh, that's worse lying back." It eases again when you sit up and lean forward.
  • If they order pain relief, the nurse gives what is ordered and by the end of Part 1 the pain has eased a little, to about 5/10 (and to 4/10 by the 00:50 obs).
  • If they explain what they are doing in plain words, you relax and say thank you.

Opening line: "I've got this pain in my chest that just won't go away, and I can't get comfortable."

History (give only when asked):

The pain

  • Site: "right behind the centre of my chest".
  • Radiation: "I also felt it in my neck."
  • Onset: earlier today. You were not exercising and had no injury. "I can't pinpoint an exact moment, but it came on pretty suddenly."
  • Time course: it built up quickly after it started and has been constant ever since.
  • Character: sharp and stabbing.
  • Severity: 7/10.
  • Worse: breathing in deeply, coughing, and lying down. You could not sleep because lying down makes it worse.
  • Better: sitting up and leaning forward.
  • Not related to: eating, exertion, or pressing on your chest.
  • Compared with before: nothing like this has ever happened to you. It is different from your occasional heartburn, and Mylanta has not helped it.

Other symptoms

  • Fever: you have felt hot and sweaty, as if you had a temperature. No night sweats and no weight loss.
  • Sick contacts: your 3-year-old son goes to day-care and had a fever about 10 days ago.
  • Negatives (say no if asked): no shortness of breath, no cough, no coughing up blood, no palpitations, no fainting or dizziness, no ankle swelling, no nausea, no vomiting or retching, no cold sweat with the pain, no trouble swallowing, no black stools, no change in bowel habit, no tearing pain going through to the back.
  • Heart risk factors (say no if asked): no high blood pressure, diabetes or high cholesterol that you know of; your blood pressure and cholesterol were normal at a GP check last year.
  • Clot risk (say no if asked): no calf pain or leg swelling, no previous clots, no recent surgery, long trips or time laid up in bed.
  • Other systems (say no if asked): no rashes, joint pains or muscle aches, no kidney problems, no injury to the chest, no recent severe stress, and no history of anxiety or panic attacks.

Past medical history

  • Asthma as a child. You have not needed a reliever puffer for many years.
  • Occasional heartburn.
  • Your only hospital stay was for the birth of your son, with no complications.
  • If asked, you weigh about 64 kg.

Medications

  • No regular prescription medicines.
  • Mylanta over the counter for occasional heartburn. It has not helped this pain.
  • Contraception: an Implanon (progestogen) implant. If asked, your periods are light and irregular on it, and you do not think you could be pregnant.
  • No vitamins or supplements.
  • If asked about anti-inflammatories: you have taken Nurofen for period pain before and it never affected your breathing.

Allergies: none.

Family history: nothing of note. Your father, mother and younger sister are all healthy. Nobody in the family has had early heart disease or autoimmune disease.

Social history

  • Non-smoker. You do not drink alcohol.
  • You tried cannabis a couple of times at university. No other recreational drugs, ever.
  • You work as a software engineer. The job is sedentary, but you walk the dog every day.
  • Your partner cooks varied, generally healthy food.
  • You live in a rented home with your partner, your dog and your 3-year-old son, who goes to day-care. You feel safe and supported at home. Your partner is at home with your son tonight.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: "The pain is bad enough that it must be something serious." You are worried it is your heart. You would like to know what is going on, to have something for the pain so that you can sleep, and to get home to your son if it is safe.

Exam findings (give only when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: tired, uncomfortable young woman sitting up and leaning forward. Slightly flushed. Speaking in full sentences, with no increased work of breathing. Not pale and not clammy.
  • Vital signs: as at triage. Temperature 37.8 °C.
  • Pulse: 104/min, regular, normal volume.
  • Blood pressure: right arm 130/80 mmHg, left arm 128/78 mmHg. No pulsus paradoxus (less than 10 mmHg fall on inspiration).
  • JVP: not raised.
  • Heart: apex beat not displaced. Heart sounds dual and not muffled. No murmurs. A scratchy, high-pitched, superficial sound at the left lower sternal edge, heard best with her sitting forward and holding her breath out. It does not change when she holds her breath.
  • Chest: trachea central. Expansion equal. Percussion resonant on both sides. Vesicular breath sounds with no crackles, no wheeze and no pleural rub.
  • Chest wall and neck: no tenderness on palpation, and pressing does not reproduce the pain. No surgical emphysema in the neck or chest wall. No rash or vesicles.
  • Abdomen: soft and non-tender, including the epigastrium.
  • Legs: calves soft and non-tender. No swelling or ankle oedema.
  • Joints and skin: no joint swelling and no rash.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self as the intern, confirms Farihah's identity and gains consent.
Acknowledges her pain and offers analgesia early. Lets her sit forward for comfort, uses plain language, and responds with empathy to her worry that this must be serious.
History
Characterises the chest pain:

kids.x: Site and radiation: retrosternal, spreading to the neck
Onset and course: fairly sudden earlier today, with no trauma or exertion, building quickly and then constant
Pleuritic and positional: worse with deep breathing, coughing and lying down, better sitting up and leaning forward

check.x: Establishes that this is a first episode, different from her usual heartburn and not relieved by Mylanta.
Asks about a preceding infection: fever or feeling hot and sweaty, cough, and sick contacts (son febrile at day-care about 10 days ago).
Asks about cardiac symptoms and coronary risk: nausea, sweating with the pain, palpitations, syncope and ankle swelling; hypertension, diabetes, cholesterol and smoking.

Screens for pulmonary embolism: breathlessness, haemoptysis, unilateral calf pain or swelling, previous DVT, immobilisation or recent surgery, and hormonal contraception (identifies the progestogen-only implant).
Asks about GI and oesophageal causes: link to eating, vomiting or retching before the pain, dysphagia, melaena and heartburn history.

Asks about at least one further cluster for other causes of pericarditis or chest pain: rash, arthralgia, myalgia or family autoimmune disease (connective tissue disease); kidney disease (uraemia); chest trauma; anxiety or panic.
Takes the past history: childhood asthma with no reliever for many years, occasional heartburn, and only hospital stay for her son's birth.
Takes the medication and allergy history needed before prescribing:

kids.x: No regular medicines, Mylanta over the counter, Implanon, no supplements; no allergies
Previous NSAID use without bronchospasm, given her asthma history, and whether she could be pregnant

check.x: Takes a family history: parents and sister healthy, no premature cardiovascular disease.
Takes a social history: smoking, alcohol and recreational drugs, occupation, and who is at home (partner and 3-year-old son).
Explores ideas, concerns and expectations: thinks it must be serious, worried about her heart, wants pain relief and to get home to her son.
Examination
Asks early to see the 12-lead ECG (to exclude STEMI), and asks the nurse for IV access and bloods including a troponin.
Does a general inspection and reviews the vital signs: uncomfortable, sitting forward, flushed; temperature 37.8 °C, HR 105.
Looks for tamponade and dissection: pulse, BP in both arms (equal), pulsus paradoxus (absent), JVP (not raised) and whether the heart sounds are muffled (they are not).
Auscultates the precordium (ideally with her sitting forward in held expiration) and names the finding as a pericardial friction rub at the left lower sternal edge.
Examines the respiratory system (trachea, expansion, percussion, auscultation): no signs of pneumothorax, consolidation or pleural rub.
Palpates the chest wall (pain not reproduced), looks for a rash or vesicles and surgical emphysema, and examines the abdomen.
Examines the calves for DVT and the ankles for oedema.
Interpretation
Interprets the observations: haemodynamically stable, not hypoxic, mild tachycardia and temperature below 38 °C, pain improving with analgesia.
Reads the ECG systematically:

kids.x: Sinus rhythm about 98/min with no pathological Q waves.
Widespread concave (saddle-shaped) ST elevation in I, II, aVF and V2 to V6, with ST depression only in aVR and V1
PR segment depression, with PR elevation in aVR.

check.x: States that the ECG fits acute pericarditis rather than STEMI, giving at least three of: ST elevation in both limb and chest leads that does not fit one coronary territory; PR depression; reciprocal change only in aVR and V1; concave ST segments; no Q waves.
Interprets the inflammatory markers: CRP 46, ESR 34 and mild neutrophilia show systemic inflammation, which supports the diagnosis and gives a baseline to guide treatment.
Interprets the normal hs-troponin I on arrival and at 2 hours (3 and 3 ng/L, below 16) as showing no myocardial injury. This argues against myocardial infarction and myopericarditis.
Interprets the other bloods: low pre-test probability (Wells 4 or below, PE unlikely) with a normal D-dimer excludes PE; negative beta-hCG and normal renal function allow NSAID and colchicine.
check.d: Accept a comment on lipase or PERC as a bonus only; it is not needed for the mark.

check.x: Interprets the chest X-ray as normal: no pneumothorax, consolidation, widened mediastinum, pneumomediastinum or effusion. States that a normal heart size does not exclude a pericardial effusion.

Gives acute pericarditis, probably viral or idiopathic, as the most likely diagnosis. Justifies it with at least two of the four criteria (she has three: characteristic pain, a friction rub and typical ECG changes), with the viral contact, low-grade fever and no cardiovascular risk factors.

Gives differentials across systems, each with a feature for or against: at least one life-threatening cardiac cause (ACS/STEMI, aortic dissection, myocarditis), one pulmonary cause (PE, pneumothorax) and one oesophageal cause (rupture).
Management

Asks for senior ED review and an echocardiogram (bedside echo tonight, with a formal TTE to follow; either earns the mark) to look for a pericardial effusion or tamponade before deciding on disposition.
Prescribes an NSAID: ibuprofen 600 mg orally 8-hourly with food (or high-dose aspirin), checking first that she has no NSAID-sensitive asthma and is not pregnant.
check.d: Credit "for 1 to 2 weeks until pain and CRP settle, then taper" if it comes here or in question 4 (item 46 covers the taper).

check.x: Adds colchicine 500 micrograms orally once daily (she weighs under 70 kg; twice daily if 70 kg or more) for 3 months to reduce recurrence, and warns about diarrhoea.
Adds a proton pump inhibitor for gastroprotection while she takes the NSAID, given her heartburn.

Does not activate the STEMI pathway and does not give thrombolysis, anticoagulation (heparin/enoxaparin) or dual antiplatelet therapy (thrombolysis or anticoagulation risks bleeding into the pericardium). Anti-inflammatory high-dose aspirin, or a single aspirin 300 mg given before the troponin is back, does not lose this mark.
check.d: Credit stating that corticosteroids are not first-line as an accepted extra; it is not required.

check.x: States that she has no high-risk features, naming at least two (e.g. temperature below 38 °C, normal troponin, no effusion on echo), so she can be discharged with early GP review; admits if any are present.
Safety netting

Explains in plain words that the lining sac around the heart is inflamed, probably after a virus, that the heart muscle is not damaged and that this is not a heart attack, and checks her understanding.
Tells her to call 000 or return to ED straight away for worsening chest pain, breathlessness, feeling faint or light-headed, a racing heart, or new swelling of the legs or belly.

Tells her to see her GP or return if she has a fever over 38 °C or is not improving after a week, or has medication side effects (any one of diarrhoea, stomach pain or black stools); advises no strenuous exercise until the pain has gone.
check.d: Taking colchicine for the full 3 months is accepted, not required.

check.x: Arranges GP review in about 1 week with a repeat CRP to guide the NSAID taper.
check.d: Echo review, cardiology referral if she relapses or does not respond, and a medical certificate are accepted extras, not required.

part2.lead: Here are her observations, the 12-lead ECG the nurse recorded, her blood results and her chest X-ray report.
part2.patient:
Ask this straight after the examiner reads question 4; the candidate answers you directly as part of question 4. Do not interrupt the safety-netting answer.

  • "So is it my heart? Can I go home tonight?"

If the candidate explains clearly and kindly, you are relieved and agree to the plan. If they use jargon such as "pericardium", ask: "What does that actually mean?"

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Room air throughout; the first two sets before medical review, the 00:50 set after analgesia. CRT 2 seconds.
handover.model:
• Read: RR 14 to 16, SpO2 99% on room air, BP 130/80, 128/78 then 126/76, HR 105, 98 then 92 and regular, temperature 37.7 to 37.9 °C, alert. Every vital sign is in the white zone. Pain 7/10 at triage, 4/10 after analgesia.
  • Meaning: she has mild tachycardia and a low-grade temperature that fit an inflammatory process. She is not shocked and not hypoxic, and her blood pressure is stable with nothing to suggest tamponade. Her temperature is below 38 °C, so fever is not one of her high-risk features.
  • Changes: the chart does not call for a clinical review or a rapid response. Pain is improving with treatment; continue regular NSAID and repeat obs 4-hourly. A falling BP, rising HR or new breathlessness would call for urgent escalation and an echo for tamponade.

rows.note: Triage ATS 2: chest pain, sitting forward
12-lead ECG recorded 22:48; cannula inserted and bloods collected; awaiting medical review
After analgesia (as charted); repeat troponin collected

handover.label: 12-lead ECG
handover.result:
12-lead ECG: Farihah Hussain, DOB 01/03/1992, recorded 21/05/2026 at 22:48 (25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV).

  • Rate: 98/min.
  • Rhythm: sinus rhythm, with a P wave before every QRS and a normal P wave axis.
  • Axis: normal.
  • P waves: normal morphology.
  • PR interval and segment: PR interval 150 ms. Downsloping PR segment depression, most evident in II, aVF, V2 and V3. PR segment elevation in V1 and aVR.
  • QRS: 86 ms with normal morphology and no pathological Q waves. R wave progression normal.
  • ST segments: widespread concave (saddle-shaped) ST elevation of about 1–2 mm in I, II, aVF and V2 to V6 (III and aVL isoelectric or minimally elevated); ST depression only in aVR and V1.
  • T waves: normal morphology.
  • QTc: 410 ms (Bazett).
  • Comparison: no previous ECG on file.
handover.model:
• Read: confirms the patient details and date. Sinus rhythm at 98/min with a normal axis, normal P waves, normal PR, QRS and QTc intervals, and no Q waves. Widespread concave ST elevation of about 1–2 mm in I, II, aVF and V2 to V6, with III and aVL isoelectric or minimally elevated, and ST depression only in aVR and V1. PR depression in II, aVF, V2 and V3 with PR elevation in V1 and aVR. Normal T waves.
  • Meaning: widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression is stage 1 acute pericarditis. ST elevation in both limb and chest leads that does not fit one coronary territory, PR depression, reciprocal change only in aVR and V1, concave ST segments and no Q waves all argue against STEMI.
  • Changes: with her pleuritic, positional pain and the rub, this meets three of the four diagnostic criteria. Do not activate the STEMI pathway. Repeat the ECG if the pain changes in character. The ECG is expected to evolve over the next days to weeks.

handover.label: Bloods
handover.result: Venous sample collected 22:50, with a repeat hs-troponin at 00:50.
handover.model:
• Read: CRP 46 and ESR 34 are raised, and WCC 11.6 with neutrophils 7.9 is a mild neutrophilia. hs-troponin I is 3 ng/L on arrival and 3 ng/L at 2 hours, below the women's 99th percentile of 16, with no rise. D-dimer is 0.32 (normal). Urea, creatinine, electrolytes and lipase are normal. Serum beta-hCG is negative.
  • Meaning: there is systemic inflammation, which fits acute pericarditis. Two normal troponins show no myocardial injury, which argues strongly against MI and against myopericarditis. PERC cannot be applied because her HR was 105 at triage. Her Wells score is 1.5 (PE unlikely), and a normal D-dimer excludes PE. Normal renal function excludes uraemic pericarditis, and a normal lipase argues against pancreatitis.
  • Changes: a normal troponin removes one high-risk feature. The negative pregnancy test and normal renal function make ibuprofen and colchicine safe to start. CRP is the baseline used to guide the length of NSAID treatment and the taper.

handover.label: Chest X-ray
handover.result:
Examination: chest X-ray, PA erect, 23:20.

Clinical details: 34-year-old woman with sharp pleuritic, positional central chest pain and low-grade fever. ?Pneumothorax ?pneumonia ?mediastinal pathology.

Findings:

  • Lungs: clear, with no consolidation, collapse or mass. Normal pulmonary vasculature.
  • Pleura: no pneumothorax and no pleural effusion. Costophrenic angles sharp.
  • Heart and mediastinum: cardiothoracic ratio within normal limits and normal cardiac contour. Mediastinum not widened, with a normal aortic contour. No pneumomediastinum. Trachea central.
  • Diaphragm: normal. No free subdiaphragmatic gas.
  • Bones and soft tissues: no fracture. No surgical emphysema.

Conclusion: normal chest X-ray.
handover.model:
• Read: an adequate PA film with clear lungs, no pneumothorax or effusion, normal heart size and contour, a mediastinum that is not widened, no pneumomediastinum or surgical emphysema, and no free gas.
  • Meaning: this argues against pneumothorax, pneumonia and oesophageal rupture, and makes aortic dissection less likely. A normal cardiac silhouette does not exclude a pericardial effusion, because an effusion has to be fairly large before the heart shadow enlarges.
  • Changes: a transthoracic echo is still needed to look for an effusion or tamponade before deciding on disposition.

ask: You are now calling the emergency registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Farihah Hussain, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Farihah now, here in the emergency department.
Before Farihah goes home, what would you tell her and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, ED intern; Farihah Hussain, 34.
  • Situation: sharp retrosternal chest pain since earlier today, 7/10 (now 4/10 after analgesia), radiating to the neck, pleuritic, worse lying down and better sitting forward. Vital signs white zone, HR 105 settling to 92, afebrile below 38 °C, SpO2 99% RA.
  • Background: son febrile 10 days ago; no cardiovascular risk factors; childhood asthma, heartburn, Implanon; no allergies.
  • Assessment: pericardial rub, no tamponade signs. ECG: sinus rhythm 98, concave ST elevation in I, II, aVF and V2 to V6 with depression only in aVR and V1, PR depression with PR elevation in aVR, no Q waves: not one coronary territory, a pericarditis pattern. CRP 46, ESR 34; troponin 3 then 3 (normal); D-dimer normal with low Wells (PE excluded); beta-hCG negative and normal renal function (safe for NSAID and colchicine); CXR normal, but a normal heart size does not exclude an effusion. Acute pericarditis with no high-risk features.
  • Recommendation: please review; bedside echo for effusion; agree on ibuprofen with colchicine and discharge if echo normal.

Acute pericarditis, probably viral or idiopathic: sharp pleuritic, positional pain, a friction rub, and widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression (3 of 4 criteria), with a viral contact, low-grade fever, raised CRP and no risk factors.

  • STEMI/ACS: against: no risk factors, pain is not ischaemic, ST elevation in limb and chest leads does not fit one territory, PR depression, normal troponins.
  • Myocarditis/myopericarditis: for: viral illness; against: normal troponin.
  • Aortic dissection: against: no tearing pain to the back, equal BP in both arms, normal mediastinum.
  • PE: for: pleuritic pain, HR 105; against: no breathlessness or DVT risk, Wells 1.5, normal D-dimer.
  • Oesophageal rupture: against: no vomiting or retching, no surgical emphysema, normal CXR.

1. Senior ED review; analgesia now; let her sit forward.
  2. Echo (bedside tonight, with a formal TTE to follow; either earns the mark) for effusion or tamponade.
  3. Ibuprofen 600 mg orally 8-hourly with food for 1 to 2 weeks, until pain resolves and CRP normalises, then taper. Checked: no NSAID-sensitive asthma, beta-hCG negative.
  4. Colchicine 500 micrograms once daily (64 kg, under 70 kg) for 3 months.
  5. PPI for gastroprotection (history of heartburn).
  6. No STEMI pathway, thrombolysis, anticoagulation or dual antiplatelet therapy (risk of bleeding into the pericardium); anti-inflammatory aspirin or a single aspirin 300 mg before the troponin is back is acceptable.
  7. Disposition: no high-risk features (temperature below 38 °C, acute onset, normal troponin, not immunosuppressed, no anticoagulant, no trauma) and no significant effusion: discharge with GP follow-up; otherwise admit.

• Explanation: inflammation of the lining sac around the heart, probably after a virus. The heart muscle is not damaged; most people recover over 1 to 2 weeks.
  • Call 000 or come straight back for worse chest pain, breathlessness, feeling faint, a racing heart, or new leg or belly swelling.
  • See the GP or return for a fever over 38 °C, no improvement after a week, or diarrhoea, stomach pain or black stools; no strenuous exercise until the pain has gone.
  • Follow-up: GP in about 1 week with a repeat CRP to guide the taper.

ddx.for: Sharp retrosternal pleuritic pain that is worse lying down and better sitting forward, a friction rub, widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression, a febrile son 10 days ago, temperature 37.8 °C and CRP 46.
ddx.against: Normal troponins and a normal chest X-ray do not argue against it, but it remains a diagnosis of exclusion until its mimics are ruled out.

ddx.dx: ST-elevation myocardial infarction or other acute coronary syndrome
ddx.for: She has central chest pain radiating to the neck and ST elevation in I, II, aVF and V2 to V6.
ddx.against: She is 34 with no cardiovascular risk factors, the pain is sharp, pleuritic and positional, the ST elevation spans limb and chest leads without fitting one coronary territory, with PR depression and no Q waves, and hs-troponin is normal at 0 and 2 hours.

ddx.for: A recent viral contact, low-grade fever, tachycardia and ST changes.
ddx.against: hs-troponin is normal and unchanged at 3 ng/L, and she has no breathlessness, palpitations or signs of heart failure.

ddx.for: Sudden-onset severe central chest pain radiating to the neck.
ddx.against: The pain is not tearing and does not go to the back, BP is equal in both arms, and the mediastinum is not widened on the chest X-ray.

ddx.for: Pleuritic chest pain with HR 105 at triage, so PERC cannot be used.
ddx.against: She has no breathlessness, haemoptysis, calf symptoms, previous clot, immobility or oestrogen, SpO2 is 99%, Wells is 1.5 and the D-dimer is normal.

ddx.for: Severe retrosternal pain radiating to the neck, with a history of heartburn.
ddx.against: She had no vomiting or retching beforehand, there is no surgical emphysema, and the chest X-ray shows no pneumomediastinum or effusion.

guide:
If the candidate did not order analgesia in Part 1, tell them the triage nurse gave paracetamol 1 g orally under the standing order at 23:00. In Part 1, Farihah answers the history and the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they examine. Describe the friction rub only if the candidate listens to the heart. If they say they listen with her sitting forward in expiration, describe it clearly. If they listen only with her lying flat, say that she cannot lie flat because of the pain. If they auscultate without stating position, she is already sitting forward, so describe the rub. Award item 21 if the candidate names the sound as a pericardial (friction) rub. Asking for sitting forward in held expiration is expected but is not required for the mark. A candidate who describes a scratchy sound but does not name it as a rub does not get item 21. If the candidate asks for the ECG, bloods or chest X-ray in Part 1, say they will be given in Part 2. Item 18 needs both: asking to see the ECG early and asking for IV access with bloods including a troponin.

In Part 2, hand over all four results, then ask the four questions in order. Farihah's question comes straight after question 4 is read, and the candidate answers her as part of question 4. Credit a systematic ECG read whether it comes before the handover or within it. If the candidate asks for an echo result, say the ED consultant's bedside echo shows no pericardial effusion and normal left ventricular function. For item 31, comments on lipase or PERC are a bonus only.

The history marks follow the source's systems-review scheme. A strong candidate covers the general, cardiovascular, respiratory and GI clusters and at least one more (rheumatological, renal, trauma or psychiatric). A candidate who asks only cardiac questions should not get items 9 to 11.

A high-performing candidate draws out the sharp, pleuritic, positional pain and the viral contact. They screen systematically for ACS, PE, dissection and oesophageal causes, check whether she could be pregnant and whether NSAIDs have affected her asthma before prescribing, and find the rub with her sitting forward. In Part 2 they read the ECG systematically and explain why it is pericarditis and not STEMI. They use the normal troponin and D-dimer correctly and give a differential across the cardiac, pulmonary and GI systems. They prescribe ibuprofen with colchicine and a PPI, ask for an echo, decide disposition on high-risk features, and safety-net in plain words.

A borderline candidate calls the ECG "ST elevation, so STEMI" and activates the cath lab or gives thrombolysis, anticoagulation or dual antiplatelet therapy. Or they reassure without excluding the mimics, give only cardiac differentials, omit colchicine or the echo, or send her home without clear return advice.
explain:
Diagnosis: acute pericarditis

Farihah has acute pericarditis, most likely viral or idiopathic, which are the commonest causes in Australia. The diagnosis is clinical and needs at least two of four criteria:

  1. characteristic chest pain, which is sharp, pleuritic, worse lying flat and better sitting forward
  2. a pericardial friction rub
  3. characteristic ECG changes
  4. a new or worsening pericardial effusion on imaging.

She has the first three. A febrile child at day-care 10 days before, a low-grade temperature and raised CRP and ESR all support a viral cause. Because its mimics are life-threatening, pericarditis is a diagnosis of exclusion.

A safety-first approach to chest pain

In acute presentations, examiners are asking whether they would trust you as an intern. Approach the history as a way of judging how likely the immediately life-threatening causes are:

  • Cardiovascular: acute coronary syndromes, aortic dissection, cardiac tamponade, and Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy.
  • Pulmonary: pulmonary embolism and tension pneumothorax.
  • Oesophageal: rupture and impaction.

Keeping these in mind guides the focused questions and reminds you that senior review is usually needed. An anatomical approach helps with pleuritic pain. Pain that moves with breathing comes from anything touching the pleura: the lung parenchyma, mediastinum (pericardium, oesophagus), diaphragm, the structures under the diaphragm (liver, spleen) and the chest wall. Other differentials are pneumonia or pleurisy, GORD, oesophagitis, pancreatitis, costochondritis and herpes zoster. The history covers the general, cardiovascular, respiratory and GI clusters, plus rheumatological symptoms (connective tissue disease causing serositis), renal disease (uraemic pericarditis), trauma and anxiety.

Examination

Listen with the patient sitting forward in held expiration. A pericardial rub is scratchy and superficial, and it persists when the breath is held, which separates it from a pleural rub. It is often intermittent, so its absence does not exclude pericarditis. Always look for tamponade: hypotension, a raised JVP, muffled heart sounds and pulsus paradoxus. Compare the BP in both arms for dissection, and look for surgical emphysema, chest wall tenderness, a zoster rash and a DVT.

The ECG

Stage 1 acute pericarditis shows widespread ST elevation, often with reciprocal ST depression in aVR and V1, and PR segment depression with PR elevation in aVR. Over the next week the segments return to baseline and the T waves flatten (stage 2). The T waves may then invert (stage 3) before the ECG returns to normal (stage 4). A downsloping TP segment (Spodick sign) supports pericarditis but is not diagnostic on its own.

Features that favour pericarditis over STEMI are:

  • ST elevation that does not fit one coronary territory
  • concave (saddle-shaped) ST segments
  • PR depression
  • no reciprocal ST depression apart from aVR and V1
  • no Q waves
  • a normal troponin.

In Farihah's ECG, concave ST elevation in both limb leads (I, II, aVF) and chest leads (V2 to V6), with ST depression only in aVR and V1, PR depression and PR elevation in aVR, does not fit a single coronary territory.

Investigations

eTG recommends investigating all suspected pericarditis with:

  • an ECG
  • a chest X-ray and a transthoracic echocardiogram
  • inflammatory markers (WCC, CRP, ESR)
  • troponin, for myocardial injury.

A raised troponin suggests myopericarditis, which is a high-risk feature. Her troponins are normal. The echo looks for an effusion and tamponade, and a normal chest X-ray does not exclude an effusion.

PE needs a structured approach. PERC cannot be used because her HR was 105 at triage. Her Wells score is 1.5 (PE unlikely), so a normal D-dimer excludes PE. Before an NSAID and colchicine are started, a pregnancy test and renal function are checked.

Management (eTG, Pericarditis)

  • NSAID: ibuprofen 600 mg orally 8-hourly with food, or high-dose aspirin as an alternative. Continue until symptoms resolve and CRP normalises, usually 1 to 2 weeks, then taper. Check for NSAID-sensitive asthma and pregnancy first.
  • Colchicine: add colchicine 500 micrograms orally twice daily, or once daily under 70 kg, for 3 months. It halves the recurrence rate. The common side effect is diarrhoea.
  • Gastroprotection: a proton pump inhibitor while on the NSAID, particularly with her heartburn history.
  • Corticosteroids: not first-line. They are kept for contraindications to NSAIDs or for specific causes, because they increase recurrence.
  • Activity: restrict physical activity beyond ordinary daily life until symptoms resolve and CRP normalises. Competitive athletes need longer.

The 2025 ESC Guidelines for the management of myocarditis and pericarditis, which replace the 2015 ESC pericardial guideline, keep an NSAID or aspirin with colchicine as first-line treatment for acute pericarditis.

Disposition

High-risk features that call for admission are:

  • fever above 38 °C
  • a subacute onset
  • a large effusion or tamponade
  • failure to respond to an NSAID after a week
  • myopericarditis (raised troponin)
  • immunosuppression
  • trauma
  • oral anticoagulant therapy.

Patients without these features and with no significant effusion can be treated as outpatients with early GP review.

Safety netting and follow-up

Tell her to call 000 or return for worsening pain, breathlessness, presyncope, palpitations or new swelling, which may mean tamponade or myocardial involvement. She should see her GP or return for a high fever, no improvement after a week, or medication side effects. GP review at about 1 week with a repeat CRP guides the NSAID taper. Colchicine continues for 3 months. Recurrence or a poor response needs cardiology referral.
points: Pericarditis pain is sharp, pleuritic and positional: worse lying flat and eased by sitting forward. Acute pericarditis needs 2 of 4 criteria: typical pain, a friction rub, typical ECG changes and a pericardial effusion.

Acute pericarditis on ECG shows widespread concave ST elevation not confined to one coronary territory, PR depression (PR elevation in aVR) and reciprocal change only in aVR and V1, with no Q waves. Read every ST elevation ECG systematically before calling it STEMI.

Pericarditis is a diagnosis of exclusion. Screen for the life-threatening chest pain causes in every system: ACS, dissection, tamponade and Takotsubo; PE and tension pneumothorax; oesophageal rupture and impaction.

eTG/ESC investigations are an ECG, a chest X-ray, a transthoracic echo, inflammatory markers and troponin. A raised troponin means myopericarditis, a high-risk feature, and a normal chest X-ray does not exclude an effusion.

Treat with an NSAID (ibuprofen 600 mg 8-hourly, tapered once pain and CRP settle), colchicine for 3 months (500 micrograms once daily under 70 kg, twice daily from 70 kg) and gastroprotection. Corticosteroids are not first-line.

Admit if there are high-risk features: fever above 38 °C, subacute onset, a large effusion or tamponade, a raised troponin, immunosuppression, trauma, anticoagulants or failure of NSAIDs. Otherwise discharge with clear red flags and GP review with a repeat CRP.
